title: How Alumin(i)um Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore aluminum (spelled aluminium in British usage), covering its naming history from Humphrey Davy's "illuminium" through the 1886 Hall-Héroult process and Carl Josef Bayer's 1887 refining method, its early luxury status (Napoleon III, the 1884 aluminum Washington Monument cap), and its use in airplanes (Wright brothers' engine), electrical wiring, beer and soft drink cans, and foil. They discuss recycling of aluminum cans, health concerns (antiperspirants, Alzheimer's research), the Goldman Sachs aluminum warehouse hoarding controversy, and environmental costs of bauxite mining. The episode closes with a listener mail about airplane aisle-seat etiquette.

segments.title: Tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming tour dates in Orlando, Nashville and Atlanta and point to ticket links.

segments.title: Opening banter on aluminum
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as the second in their series on the periodic table elements and note aluminum's ubiquity and recent discovery compared with copper, iron and bronze.

segments.title: Abundance and early uses of alum
segments.summary: Aluminum makes up about eight percent of Earth's crust but is locked in bauxite ore and hard to extract. Alum (potassium aluminum sulfate) and aluminum-bearing clay were used for thousands of years, and an alleged out-of-place aluminum belt from a third-century tomb in China is discussed.

segments.title: Discovery and isolation of aluminum
segments.summary: Lavoisier suspected an aluminum oxide base; Humphrey Davy named the element and wrote about it before isolation. Ørsted came close in 1825 with impure metal, and Wöhler produced pure aluminum two years later.

segments.title: Spelling aluminum vs aluminium
segments.summary: Davy's spelling changed from illuminium to aluminum; British chemists later preferred aluminium, while Americans kept aluminum until the American Chemical Society adopted it in 1925.

segments.title: Luxury metal era and Washington Monument cap
segments.summary: Aluminum was costly to extract and called the metal of kings; Napoleon III reportedly had special cutlery. The 1884 Washington Monument aluminum pyramid cap represented a large share of world output that year.

segments.title: Hall-Héroult process and Bayer process
segments.summary: Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult independently developed the electrolytic process in 1886, sharing credit; Karl Josef Bayer improved aluminum oxide extraction from bauxite in 1887, making industrial production practical.

segments.title: Pittsburgh Reduction Company and falling prices
segments.summary: Hall helped found what became the Aluminum Company of America (Alcoa), and the price of aluminum fell sharply from the late 1880s through the 1930s.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Electricity, dams and aluminum alloys
segments.summary: Aluminum smelting is energy intensive, so early plants were sited near dams and the growing electrical grid helped the industry. Pure aluminum is soft, so it is alloyed with iron, silicon and copper for strength.

segments.title: Aluminum in aviation
segments.summary: The Wright brothers' engine used about 92 percent aluminum and 8 percent copper, built by mechanic Charlie Taylor. Aluminum later replaced wood and fabric in airplanes and was valued for its strength-to-weight ratio.

segments.title: Aluminum wiring and fire hazards
segments.summary: Aluminum conducts less well than copper and needs a larger diameter. Aluminum household wiring from the 1960s and 1970s loosened at connections and posed arcing and fire risks.

segments.title: Beer and soda can history
segments.summary: Hawaii Brewing Company tried aluminum cans for Primo beer in the late 1950s but failed due to a can-lining reaction; Coors perfected the can in 1959, followed by soft drink makers.

segments.title: Aluminum can recycling
segments.summary: About 20 percent of global aluminum goes to cans; cans are infinitely recyclable with about 5 percent of the carbon emissions. Only about 50 percent of cans are recycled, and about 75 percent of all aluminum ever produced is still in use.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Aluminum foil and tinfoil hats
segments.summary: Aluminum foil was used for candy packaging from 1910 and hit the US in 1913. The tinfoil hat idea traces to a 1927 Aldous Huxley story, World War II propaganda, and a 2005 MIT study found foil does not block electromagnetic signals.

segments.title: Aluminum foil ball challenge and vapor deposition
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the Japanese foil ball internet challenge and how aluminum is vaporized in a vacuum to coat shiny materials. Aluminum is used in buildings like the Empire State Building and in automaking, toys, medicine and makeup.

segments.title: Aluminum health concerns
segments.summary: Hosts discuss aluminum in antiperspirants, a debunked breast cancer scare, research linking aluminum to Alzheimer's-related brain changes, and the kidneys' role in clearing aluminum. Scientific debate is described as ongoing.

segments.title: Goldman Sachs aluminum hoarding
segments.summary: Goldman Sachs stored aluminum in a Detroit-area warehouse, causing delays that critics said were manufactured to raise prices. A 2021 hoarding case in Vietnam is also mentioned, along with price swings.

segments.title: Bauxite mining environmental impact
segments.summary: Bauxite strip mining depletes land, pollutes water with heavy metals, and produces about three percent of the world's direct CO2 emissions. Recycling is encouraged, and the Washington Monument cap is said to have been proposed for melting in World War II.

segments.title: Transition to listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts announce listener mail.

segments.title: Airplane aisle seat etiquette
segments.summary: A listener named Frank describes asking a passenger to be let past repeatedly on a Delta comfort plus flight; hosts discuss whether Frank was rude and offer views on aisle-seat etiquette.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts plug Max Fun Network and invite listener mail, then sign off.
